title: Angular Momentum Calculator L = I·ω | Hacé Cuentas
description: Calculate angular momentum L of a rotating body from moment of inertia I (kg·m²) and angular velocity ω (rad/s) using L = I·ω. Free physics tool.
intro:
Angular momentum (L) is one of the most important conserved quantities in physics, governing everything from the spin of figure skaters to the rotation of galaxies. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, it is calculated with the deceptively compact formula L = I × ω, where I is the moment of inertia (in kg·m²) — a measure of how mass is distributed relative to the rotation axis — and ω is the angular velocity (in radians per second). The result has units of kg·m²/s, equivalent to the joule-second (J·s) used in quantum mechanics.

This calculator handles the linear rotational case and is designed for physics and engineering students, mechanical designers, robotics engineers, and educators who need quick numerical answers without breaking out a textbook. You enter the moment of inertia and angular velocity; it returns the angular momentum and a brief interpretation of the magnitude. Typical worked values: a spinning bicycle wheel (I ≈ 0.1 kg·m², ω ≈ 30 rad/s) carries L ≈ 3 kg·m²/s; a car's flywheel (I ≈ 0.5 kg·m², ω ≈ 300 rad/s) stores L ≈ 150 kg·m²/s; Earth's rotation gives L ≈ 7.07 × 10³³ kg·m²/s — staggeringly larger.

The single most powerful consequence of the formula is the Conservation of Angular Momentum: in any isolated system with no external torque, L remains constant. This is why a figure skater spins faster when pulling in their arms (smaller I forces larger ω to keep L unchanged), why a falling cat lands on its feet (precise internal redistribution of I and ω), why neutron stars rotate hundreds of times per second after collapse (collapse from R ≈ 10⁶ km to R ≈ 10 km reduces I by ~10¹⁰), and why the gyroscope on your phone can detect rotation without external reference.

Note that this calculator computes scalar angular momentum for fixed-axis rotation. The full vector form L⃗ = I·ω⃗ (with I as a tensor) is required for asymmetric bodies or precessing systems — gyroscopes, spinning tops, and rotating molecules typically need that level. For a point particle, the alternative form is L = m × v × r × sin(θ), where r is the distance from the rotation axis and θ is the angle between position and momentum vectors. Both forms reduce to the same physical quantity.

explanation:
Applied physics solves everyday problems: from free fall to household electricity. Formulas are validated by centuries of experiments.

## How It's Calculated

Angular momentum measures the rotational motion of a body. It's calculated by multiplying the moment of inertia I (resistance to rotational acceleration) by the angular velocity ω (rotational speed in radians per second).

This calculator applies the formula to your input values, checking typical ranges and alerting when values seem unusual.

## Key Points

Angular momentum is conserved in closed systems without external torque. When an ice skater pulls in their arms during a spin, their moment of inertia decreases, so their angular velocity increases to keep L constant.

This calculation is for reference. For critical decisions (medical, financial, legal), consult a professional. Data updated through 2026 and periodically reviewed.

faq.q: What is angular momentum in simple terms?
faq.a: Angular momentum (L) measures the 'amount of rotation' an object carries. For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, it equals the moment of inertia I (which captures how mass is distributed relative to the axis) multiplied by the angular velocity ω (how fast it spins, in radians per second). Its SI unit is kg·m²/s. Unlike linear momentum (p = mv) which describes straight-line motion, angular momentum describes circular or rotational motion and is conserved when no external torque acts on the system.

faq.q: Why is angular momentum conserved, and what does that mean physically?
faq.a: By Newton's second law for rotation, the rate of change of angular momentum equals the net external torque: τ = dL/dt. If τ = 0 (no external twist applied to the system), then dL/dt = 0, meaning L is constant. This is why a spinning figure skater speeds up when pulling in their arms — internal rearrangement of mass changes I, but L is conserved, forcing ω to increase. The principle also explains why planets maintain their orbital motion, why neutron stars spin so fast, and why gyroscopes resist reorientation.

faq.q: What's the difference between linear momentum and angular momentum?
faq.a: Linear momentum p = mv describes motion in a straight line, with units of kg·m/s. Angular momentum L = I·ω describes rotational motion, with units of kg·m²/s. They are independent quantities — a falling object can have zero angular momentum about its center of mass while having significant linear momentum, and a spinning top sitting still has angular momentum but zero linear momentum. Both follow analogous conservation laws (Newton's first law for linear; conservation of L for rotation in absence of torque).

faq.q: How do I calculate moment of inertia for common shapes?
faq.a: For a body rotating about an axis through its center of mass: **thin hoop or ring** I = mr²; **solid disk or cylinder** I = ½mr²; **solid sphere** I = ⅖mr²; **hollow sphere** I = ⅔mr²; **thin rod about center** I = (1/12)mL²; **thin rod about end** I = ⅓mL². For composite bodies, sum the individual contributions (parallel axis theorem: I = I_cm + md²). Reference tables in any physics textbook (Halliday, Resnick, Tipler) cover dozens of standard geometries.

faq.q: Do planets and stars have angular momentum?
faq.a: Yes, and on enormous scales. Earth's rotation gives L ≈ 7.07 × 10³³ kg·m²/s; its orbital angular momentum around the Sun is even larger at ≈ 2.66 × 10⁴⁰ kg·m²/s. The Sun itself has rotational L ≈ 1.92 × 10⁴¹ kg·m²/s. Conservation of L during stellar collapse explains pulsars: a star contracting from 10⁶ km to 10 km in radius reduces I by 10¹⁰, forcing ω to increase by the same factor — producing the ~1 ms rotation periods observed in millisecond pulsars.

faq.q: What is angular momentum in units of J·s, and why does that matter?
faq.a: Mathematically, kg·m²/s is dimensionally identical to J·s (joule-seconds). This equivalence is crucial in quantum mechanics, where Planck's constant ℏ = 1.054 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s sets the fundamental unit of angular momentum. Quantum angular momentum is quantized in multiples of ℏ: electron spin is ℏ/2, photon spin is ℏ. The classical formula L = I·ω works at macroscopic scales but breaks down for atoms, where angular momentum eigenvalues replace continuous values.

faq.q: What happens when angular momentum is not conserved?
faq.a: Angular momentum changes only when an external torque is applied: τ = dL/dt. Examples include friction at a bearing slowing a flywheel, atmospheric drag tidally locking the Moon to Earth (and slowly increasing the Moon's orbital L while reducing Earth's spin L), or a brake pad torquing a car wheel to a stop. The conservation law is exact only in isolated systems — most engineering problems involve dissipation, which transfers L (and energy) to surrounding bodies or to thermal motion.

faq.q: How is angular momentum used in spacecraft attitude control?
faq.a: Reaction wheels and control moment gyroscopes (CMGs) are the workhorses of satellite pointing. A reaction wheel is a flywheel (typical I = 0.001–0.1 kg·m²) spun by an electric motor; spinning it up applies an equal-and-opposite torque to the spacecraft, rotating it to a desired attitude without expending propellant. The International Space Station uses four large CMGs, each with L ≈ 4,760 N·m·s, providing precision pointing for science experiments and docking. When wheels 'saturate' (reach max ω), magnetic torquers or thrusters dump angular momentum back to space.

faq.q: Can angular momentum be transferred between objects?
faq.a: Yes — through external torques exchanged between bodies, angular momentum is conserved globally even when it changes for individual parts. Classic examples: tidal interaction between Earth and Moon transfers Earth's rotational L to the Moon's orbital L (Earth's day lengthens by ~2 ms per century while the Moon recedes by ~3.8 cm/year); the planet Jupiter contains ~60% of the solar system's total angular momentum despite having only 0.1% of its mass; in a collision between rotating bodies, contact friction redistributes L between them according to impact geometry.

faq.q: How does angular momentum apply to atomic and molecular physics?
faq.a: At atomic scales, angular momentum is quantized and central to chemistry and spectroscopy. Electrons in atoms have **orbital angular momentum** quantum number ℓ (giving s, p, d, f orbital shapes) and **spin angular momentum** quantum number s = 1/2. Molecules rotate with discrete L values that determine their rotational spectra in the microwave region. The conservation of angular momentum in particle decays (e.g., kaon → 2 pions) constrains which decay channels are allowed. The Stern-Gerlach experiment (1922) demonstrated spin quantization, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics.

faq.q: What is the difference between scalar and vector angular momentum?
faq.a: For a body rotating about a fixed, symmetric axis (most engineering cases), the scalar formula L = I·ω is sufficient and the direction of L is along the rotation axis by the right-hand rule. For asymmetric bodies, precession, or 3D rotation, L is a vector and I is a 3×3 inertia tensor: **L⃗ = I̅·ω⃗**, with the components computed via matrix multiplication. The vector treatment is essential for gyroscopes (where L⃗ rotates due to applied torque), spinning tops (precession), and any body whose mass distribution is not symmetric about the rotation axis.

faq.q: How accurate is this calculator and is it free to use?
faq.a: The calculator applies the exact formula L = I·ω with no approximations beyond your input precision. Results are accurate to the number of significant figures you enter. The tool is completely free, requires no sign-up, runs entirely in your browser (no data is sent to servers), and works on desktop and mobile.
